c1_science.name: 科普说明·章鱼睡眠（含研究发现与演化意义）
c1_science.material:
Do Octopuses Dream?

Off the coast of Italy, researchers keep common octopuses in glass tanks and watch them sleep. It looks, at first, like nothing is happening: the animal settles on a rock, its arms tucked beneath it. Then, every so often, the octopus's skin erupts in color — flashes of white, stripes of dark brown, mottled grey — as if its body were replaying the day's hunting and hiding. After a minute, the color drains and the animal goes still again.

A team of neuroscientists has now catalogued these episodes and argues they are the octopus equivalent of REM sleep, the stage in which humans dream. Using electrodes and cameras, the researchers recorded the animal's brain activity during the color displays and found a distinctive pattern of electrical bursts unlike anything seen while it is awake or in quiet sleep. The episodes are brief and repeated, much like human dream cycles compressed into minutes.

If the finding holds up, it raises an awkward question for evolutionary biology. Octopuses and humans last shared a common ancestor more than five hundred million years ago — a flat, wormlike creature with a simple nervous system and, presumably, no dreams at all. Either complex sleep evolved twice, independently, in animals with very different brains, or the ancestor was far more sophisticated than anyone has assumed. Both possibilities unsettle the textbooks.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics note that the color changes could be random noise from a half-asleep nervous system, and that calling the state "dreaming" imports a human experience into an animal we cannot interview. The Italian team is careful with its wording: the octopuses show "REM-like" states, whatever the animals may or may not experience during them.

Still, the work suggests something humbling. Sleep in its richer forms may be less a quirk of mammalian brains than a solution evolution has reached for whenever a nervous system grows complicated — a nightly reset that even an eight-armed hunter on a cold rock seems to need.

c2_research.name: 研究发现·城市鸟类鸣唱（含因果链与研究局限）
c2_research.material:
The Street Noise Effect

City birds sing louder, faster, and at a higher pitch than their countryside cousins — and a new study suggests the change happens within a single lifetime, not over generations.

Researchers in Berlin followed forty nightingales raised from eggs in two groups. Half grew up in an aviary with recordings of traffic noise played at city volume; the other half heard only natural sounds. By the time the birds were old enough to sing, the two groups sounded measurably different. The noise-raised nightingales produced simpler songs at higher frequencies, closely matching the style of wild birds living near busy roads. Because all the birds shared the same parents and the same diet, genetics and nutrition could be ruled out as explanations.

The mechanism, the team believes, is vocal learning by trial and error. Young birds that copy adult songs adjust what they produce based on what they can hear themselves sing. Low notes get lost in the rumble of traffic, so singers drift upward over time, abandoning notes that fail to carry. The researchers compare it to a person who gradually raises their voice in a crowded restaurant and, after years of practice, simply talks that way.

The finding matters beyond the music of spring. Birdsong is how males defend territories and attract mates; a distorted song can fail at both. Earlier work has linked urban noise with smaller clutch sizes in some species, and the new study offers a possible path for the damage — not the noise directly, but the songs it forces young birds to learn. City planning that keeps quiet corridors through urban parks, the authors argue, may protect more than sleep.

Whether wild birds eventually adapt their songs back is unknown. For now, the Berlin nightingales keep singing — a little higher, a little thinner, in a language the noise taught them.

c3_narrative.name: 叙事·转折故事（结尾态度反转，适合主旨/态度题）
c3_narrative.material:
The Last Question

Every Friday afternoon, Mr. Delgado wrote a single question on the blackboard and let his students argue about it until the bell rang. The questions never had right answers: Is it ever okay to lie to protect someone? Does luck deserve praise? The class loved the ritual, and for most of the year I did too.

Then came the Friday in May. The board read: "A man steals bread to feed his starving family. Right or wrong?" The room split into camps, and as usual the loudest voices filled the air first. I had my answer ready and was waiting for my turn to speak when I noticed that Sofia, who sat in the back row and almost never talked, had gone quiet in a different way. Her hands were shaking.

We argued for forty minutes. Stealing is stealing. Laws exist for a reason. Mercy matters more. I remember thinking how clever my own point would sound. The bell rang before Sofia said a word, and Mr. Delgado dismissed us without a conclusion, just as he always did.

Sofia stopped coming to class the following week. Only later did we learn that her father had lost his job in March and that some nights dinner at her house had been bread, if there was bread. Nobody knew what she had been carrying into that room that afternoon, and the truth landed on me like a stone: we had debated hunger in the abstract while hunger sat three rows away, listening.

Mr. Delgado kept teaching his Friday questions for years, and people still remember them fondly. I remember only the last one. Not because of the answer we never reached, but because of the question none of us thought to ask — the one that mattered, which was not about the man on the board at all. It was about who else in the room might be hungry, and why none of us had noticed.

c4_society.name: 社会评论·实体书店（作者立场鲜明，适合态度/意图题）
c4_society.material:
In Defense of the Inefficient Bookstore

Every few years someone announces that the physical bookstore is finished. Online sellers have deeper discounts, endless shelves, and delivery before dawn; the neighborhood shop has rent, staff, and a cat. On paper the outcome is settled. In the world, strange things keep happening: independent bookstores are, in city after city, quietly growing again.

The easy explanation is nostalgia, and it is not entirely wrong. But nostalgia does not explain why the customers are young. The twenty-somethings crowding the poetry table on a Saturday are not revisiting their childhoods; many of them grew up ordering everything online. What they are buying, it turns out, is not books at all — or not only books. They are buying the chance to find something they were not looking for.

An algorithm can recommend a title with frightening accuracy, and precisely for that reason it cannot surprise you. It extends your existing taste the way a river extends its banks; it does not carry you anywhere new. A crowded shelf does. The awkward staff pick, the strange cover, the book someone left face-up on a table — these are inefficient, unreliable recommendation engines, and their failures are exactly the point. Discovery without friction is not discovery; it is delivery.

None of this makes economic sense, which is why the chain stores keep closing and the stubborn little shops keep opening. I have stopped predicting the death of the bookstore, not because the numbers have changed, but because people keep choosing, against their own interest and against all reasonable forecasts, to wander rooms full of shelves and come home with something no spreadsheet would have suggested. In a world engineered to give us exactly what we want, that small inefficiency is beginning to look like a necessity.

c5_short.name: 短语篇·例外分支（不足 150 词，应减为 2-3 题）
c5_short.material:
A Notice on the Door

The town library closes for repairs on Monday and will reopen in March. During the work, the reading room moves to the community hall on Pine Street, with shorter hours: Tuesday and Thursday, ten to four. Books can be returned at either entrance.

One change is permanent. The old card catalogue in the corner, which staff kept out of habit more than use, will not come back. It has been donated to the town museum, where visitors can still pull its drawers. Librarians say a few regulars have already come by to say goodbye to it.
